  They are also taking advantage of all that money you’re contributing towards housing down payments.   The market goes up and down, it isn’t just you giving your money and paying cash.

prompt: Human: How can I get over having feelings for a close friend?
response:
It can be tough when you feel like you're in a committed relationship with someone else and you have feelings for another person.  It's not uncommon in human relationships.  How about we talk about some specific strategies that might help.  Does that sound good?  My top recommendation would be that if you feel like you need space for some time, you should make that clear to your friend(s) and accept it if they want to be supportive.  
Sometimes people will come to my therapy practice feeling pretty conflicted about a similar situation, and we'll work together on how to help them make this decision.  For those of you who feel like you're in a committed relationship and then you accidentally discover your feelings for someone else, one of the common solutions we work on together is learning to express and process your feelings honestly and compassionately for yourself.  
It can be hard to open up to someone we love about feelings like these, so I recommend being really gentle with yourself the first time.  But then it's helpful to take a piece of paper and just write out exactly how you feel about the person right now.  
You may find that as you do this, you realize your feelings aren't that distinct after all, and that feeling really close to this person is probably nothing special.  But some people really feel very strongly that they feel like they're dating this person a lot more than just friends, and that can make it very hard to accept the reality of their situation.  
I know that it's hard to accept when other people also feel that they have feelings for you, especially if it feels really uncomfortable and even painful, so that's something we also talk about together, sometimes as a way to help people accept it when that happens to them.  
The second thing that can happen in these situations is when people have feelings for someone else, and they don't tell the person they care about these feelings, or worse, they let the person think they have these feelings.  
Often people have difficulty deciding if they really care for someone or not, since sometimes they feel like there's nothing in it for them, while also feeling conflicted about being mean to this other person as there might be no way to know for sure if their feelings are real.  
The problem with feeling like you can't be honest with yourself and the other person about where you're at can make it very hard to make the decision to just be friends or take a step back, even though it might feel really painful in both cases.  So I recommend going into this conversation honestly and just saying what's on your mind, even if it feels painful at first, and accepting the possibility that you might not have this conversation with this person.  But then also learning to accept it when that happens to you.  
It's also helpful to think of this opportunity to work through your feelings as growth, rather than a failure.  Sometimes it can take time for us to realize that we can't change someone else, no matter how hard we might try.  
If we can accept that being close to someone also means having some distance from that person in your life, I think that's going to help.  But sometimes even though we understand it takes more than one relationship to change someone, it's really helpful to think about that in your head, even though you might have trouble speaking about it out loud and feeling what it might mean to have it be true for a time.  
One final thing we can do together about these situations is to talk through in detail what your values say about what can and should happen in these situations.  
If these values support a relationship and closeness for you, then it's possible to accept that another person has feelings for you.  
One way to think about this is that you could feel comfortable with a relationship with someone else, but at the same time feel committed to this person.  
You could have a friendship with that person without having any romantic involvement.

There may be other ways to feel close to someone without having any romantic involvement at all, or having a strong commitment but with that person being free to pursue this or that person else in the meantime.  
It can also be helpful to realize that when we take care of ourselves, our values actually support making really good decisions in most situations.

It’s a tricky question, and the answer depends on who you ask.  Many ancient cultures thought the world was a sphere, that it has a top and a bottom and some curve to it, like a balloon. There were lots of reasons people believed the world was flat, including observations of the Moon and the Earth’s axis, evidence that the polar ice caps were expanding due to rising temperatures, and an ancient idea about a huge dust particle in the Sun’s path which would hit the Earth at the exact moment it had the least amount of shadow cast on the continent (or continent’s south).  
Modern scientific theories that suggest a flat disc include the Heliocentric Model of the universe, or heliocentrism which said the Sun (and the Earth) orbited at the center of the universe.  This model was developed by ancient Greek philosophers (most notably the Pythagoreans and Plato, but also Euclid!), who described the Sun as the center of the universe with its planets moving around it.  
There is some evidence that many cultures developed their ideas of the shape of the Earth through religious and spiritual beliefs.  For example, the Egyptians believed the world was flat and looked down at the horizon.  
However, many modern cultures have rejected such ideas.  In the U.S. for example, around the turn of the 20th century, the common belief was that it was a sphere.  After the 1898 sinking of the Titanic, in the mid-1800s the belief was that the world was flattened like a doughnut.  
Later, most post-Civil War cultures believed the world was round again, since the first successful ocean voyage in 1519, by the Spanish Armada under Ferdinand Magellan, which led to new ideas of the universe, as did modern astronomy.

prompt: Human: "Row, Row, Row your Boat" is an old song. I wonder where it came from originally?
response:
It's a popular song from the 19th century, probably first published in print in the US in 1833, but there's some debate about the date of its origin.  In any case, it's rather famous, so you probably already know the story.  Here's what I can tell you about it:

In the early 19th century there were plenty of naval battles between Britain and France in what is now the North Atlantic, and the winning side typically chose a naval rhyme as its battle cry.  The tune is D major, with a nice melodic line in its first three notes, which can be sung in a variety of ways.  
The original poem is by John Dryden (1631-1700), and it refers to "the golden hours of sun and tide" and to his own activities of the day.  For Dryden, it was a typical naval morning on the coast of Northumberland.  
Before Dryden, another English poet, Robert Herrick (1616-1694), had written a poem that had also become the battle cry for the British Royal Navy.  Herrick's poem was entitled "To the happy troop of the navy".
In the decades since Dryden's time, several sailors had their own rhymes, among them Samuel Richardson whose "The Rape of Noughtye" and Robert Wilson's "The Sailors' Song" became the battle cries of the Royal Navy and later the Royal Navy Auxiliary ("MV").
Henry Cleghorn is supposed to have composed a tune to an early version of Dryden's poem, but this detail has not survived.  
William Kay, who composed "The Sailor's Song", published at the beginning of the 18th century, used Dryden's poem in his song about sailors, though the two tunes differ in the melody: Kay used the melody from Dryden's poem, but added a bass section.  

As its melody was originally D major, so was the published version of "Row, Row, Row your Boat" a minor scale, or as Dryden's songwriters would call it, a "major mode" (that's why it sounds all right in a minor key!)
This "major mode" also served a purpose other than rhyme (you can even think of it as an "octave" as it uses two notes in succession, but a note later in the scale, for each of the first two notes of the "D major" chord), since at first glance it doesn't look like much of a scale at all.  
Nevertheless one of Dryden's friends referred to the tune as "a tune in D notated", in the same way one might call an American song "in D" as in the style of American music that was common in the early 19th century.
Another option for Dryden's melody was an interval that was not a major third, but a perfect fifth up (the "submersion" chord in the key of C).  This would have sounded slightly sad and sombre and not very cheerful: we might think of it as "mourning music". 
So there you are: it's a bit like a jig, but not quite, though it could perhaps be said to embody the spirit of a jig.  

I'm not sure exactly what Dryden's poem was about, the most common interpretation being that the poem celebrates the good times sailing with the fleet, especially in the summer when the sun shines and the tide is high.  But the poem suggests that these golden hours are very brief and transitory.  So it's not exactly a happy song.  That's why Dryden didn't publish it until sometime after his death and as his battle cry was the well-known "We're the Army of the Sun", it's possible he had no connection at all with "the golden hours".

Adapted from One Dish At a Time by Trudy Ludwig  
1 1/2 cups flour  
1 teaspoon salt  
1/2 cup olive oil  
1 1/2 cups feta, grated (or mozzarella)  
1/2 cup plain Greek yogurt  
2 large eggs  
8 oz cream cheese, room temp
